title: 7 Christmas Porch Mistakes That Make Your House Look CHEAP

scenes.text: Sweetheart, people judge your house at Christmas from the street. They never see your beautiful tree, or your table, or your kitchen. They see your front porch, for about three seconds, driving by. And in those three seconds, they decide if your house looks warm, or cheap. My father knew that, and our little house on Elm Street was the warmest one on the block.
scenes.caption: THREE SECONDS

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you seven Christmas porch mistakes that make a house look cheap from the street, and the old fixes that cost almost nothing. And stay with me, because the last mistake is the one I see on almost every house in my neighborhood, and it takes five minutes to fix.
scenes.caption: SEVEN PORCH MISTAKES

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-four, my father did the outside the Saturday after Thanksgiving. A fresh wreath on the door with a red bow, a string of big colored bulbs along the edge of the porch roof, and two little cedar trees in buckets on each side of the steps. That's all. And every year, people slowed down their cars to look.
scenes.caption: PEOPLE SLOWED DOWN

scenes.text: He was a machinist, not a decorator. But he had rules. Everything even. Everything straight. And nothing that blinks. He said blinking lights belonged on a fire truck, not a family home. My mother agreed, and I've never had a blinking light on my house in eighty-two years.
scenes.caption: NOTHING THAT BLINKS

scenes.text: Mistake number one. A wreath that's too small for the door. A little twelve-inch wreath on a big front door looks like a lost button. From the street, you can't even see it. The wreath should be about two thirds the width of the door. For most front doors, that's a twenty-four inch wreath, sometimes bigger.
scenes.caption: A LOST BUTTON

scenes.text: And make your own for almost nothing. Buy a plain wreath, then tuck in branches from your yard. Pine, cedar, holly, whatever you have. Add a few pinecones and a big bow made from wired ribbon. My mother wired real red apples into hers. A plain wreath from the store looks like a store. A full one with real greens looks like a home.
scenes.caption: LOOKS LIKE A HOME

scenes.text: Mistake number two. Mixed lights. Warm white along the roof, cold blue-white on the bushes, colored on the railing, and one string blinking. From the street, it looks like a hardware store clearance aisle. Pick one kind of light for the whole outside of the house. All warm white, or all colored. Never both.
scenes.caption: A CLEARANCE AISLE

scenes.text: And hang them straight, honey. A droopy line of lights along the gutter, sagging between hooks, is the first thing people notice. Use the little plastic clips from the hardware store, one every foot, so the line is perfectly straight. My father measured with a yardstick. The neighbors laughed at him in November and admired him in December.
scenes.caption: STRAIGHT AS A YARDSTICK

scenes.text: And here's a little trick about the bulbs. The old big bulbs, the C9s, the size of your thumb, look wonderful from the street, much better than the tiny ones, which disappear from far away. They make them in LED now, so they don't get hot and they don't cost much to run. Big bulbs on the roof, small lights near the door. That's how my father did it, and it still works.
scenes.caption: BIG BULBS ON THE ROOF

scenes.text: Mistake number three. Lights only on the roofline and nothing near the door. The roof is high and far away. The door is where people come in. Put your warmest light at eye level, around the door, on the railing, in the windows, and in two lit trees or urns by the steps. That's what makes a house look welcoming instead of just bright.
scenes.caption: AT EYE LEVEL

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. In a minute I'll tell you the cheapest thing on this whole list. It costs about ten dollars, and it makes more difference than anything else you can buy.
scenes.caption: TAP THE LIKE BUTTON

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Bare steps. Here's the ten-dollar fix I promised. Two big pots or buckets on either side of the front steps, filled with cut evergreen branches standing up, a few tall birch or red dogwood sticks, and a string of little lights tucked in. It's the cheapest, prettiest thing you can do, and you can use the branches the Christmas tree lot gives away free.
scenes.caption: TEN DOLLARS

scenes.text: My father put two little live cedar trees in buckets on our steps every year, and in January he planted them in the backyard. By the time I left home, we had a row of eleven cedar trees along the back fence. Every Christmas of my childhood is still growing behind that house on Elm Street.
scenes.query: row of cedar trees backyard fence
scenes.caption: STILL GROWING

scenes.text: And don't forget the mailbox and the lamp post, honey. A little swag of greens with a red bow on the mailbox, and a wreath or a bow on the lamp post by the driveway. They're the very first things people see from the road. My father tied a small wreath to our mailbox every year, and the mailman, Mr. Hoover, told him it was the only mailbox on his route that made him smile.
scenes.caption: IT MADE HIM SMILE

scenes.text: Mistake number five. Too many things on the lawn. Inflatable snowmen, a plastic reindeer, a Santa on a motorcycle, a light-up candy cane path, and a projector throwing snowflakes on the garage. One or two of those is fun. All of them at once looks like a yard sale on fire. More isn't more, honey. Better is more.
scenes.caption: A YARD SALE ON FIRE

scenes.text: So far, a big full wreath, one kind of light, hung straight, light at eye level, and pots of greens on the steps. And here's the rule for the lawn. Pick one thing, and do it well. A single lit tree in the yard, or a pair of lit deer, or a sled leaning by the door with a wreath on it. Then leave the rest of the yard alone.
scenes.query: single lit tree front yard snow
scenes.caption: PICK ONE THING

scenes.text: Mistake number six. A muddy old doormat and a dead porch light. People forget, but the doormat is the first thing every guest looks down at. A clean, plain mat, maybe a red one or a plaid one for the season, layered on top of a bigger striped one. And put a warm bulb in the porch light. The bright white ones make the whole porch look like a gas station.
scenes.caption: NOT A GAS STATION

scenes.text: And add a lantern. A plain metal lantern with a battery candle inside, by the door or on the step. Set it on a timer, so it comes on at dusk every night. It's the one thing that makes a porch look warm from far away. My mother had an oil lantern from Grandma Pearl's farm. I still light it every Christmas Eve.
scenes.caption: GRANDMA PEARL'S LANTERN

scenes.text: And if you live in an apartment with only a balcony, sweetheart, you can still do this. A string of warm lights along the railing, clipped straight. A small wreath hung on the outside of the railing, facing the street. And one potted evergreen in the corner with a few lights. Your neighbors walking by below will look up and smile. A little balcony done right is as warm as a whole house.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE BALCONY

scenes.text: And now mistake number seven, the one I see on almost every house in my neighborhood. Coming up the walk in the dark. People spend hundreds on the roof and forget the path to their own front door. Their guests stumble up a black sidewalk to get to all those lights.
scenes.caption: A BLACK SIDEWALK

scenes.text: The five-minute fix. A row of little solar stake lights, or paper bag luminaries, along both sides of the front walk. In the fifties, we made luminaries with brown lunch bags, a cup of sand in the bottom, and a candle inside. Today use battery tea lights, so nothing catches fire. A lit path says, we're expecting you. And it keeps Aunt Margaret from falling in the bushes.
scenes.caption: WE'RE EXPECTING YOU

scenes.text: And people always ask me, when do you put it up? My father's rule was the Saturday after Thanksgiving for the outside, while it's still warm enough to stand on a ladder, and everything came down on the sixth of January. Hang the lights in November, even early November on a dry day, and just don't turn them on until after Thanksgiving. Your fingers will thank you.
scenes.caption: YOUR FINGERS WILL THANK YOU

scenes.text: And be safe out there, sweetheart. Only use lights marked for outdoor use. Plug them into an outdoor outlet with a cover, and use a timer, so they turn off at bedtime. Never staple through the wires. And always have somebody hold the ladder. My father fell off ours in nineteen sixty-two and broke his wrist, and my mother finished the lights herself with his cast pointing at her from the lawn.
scenes.caption: HOLD THE LADDER

scenes.text: So one more time. A big, full wreath, two thirds the door. One kind of light, hung straight, never blinking. The warmest light at eye level by the door. Pots of greens on the steps. One thing on the lawn, not ten. A clean mat, a warm bulb, a lantern. And a lit path to your door. That's how you make your house the warmest one on the block.
scenes.caption: THE WARMEST ON THE BLOCK

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. White lights or colored lights? I know which one I am. If you want more, the whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHITE OR COLORED?
